https://github.com/intgrah/domain-semantics-lean

I would like to share a modification of the (recently discovered) technique for proving definitional inversion in non-normalising type theories, via internalised domains in presheaves over conversion-quotiented syntactic contexts. This addresses one of the questions in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.13662 about how to scale up domain-theoretic techniques for real-world type theories. Essentially, while the the paper's model is successful for the chosen type theory, it is inadequate for axiom K, because it identifies neutrals with the bottom element, whilst axiom K allows reduction even when terms are totally stuck.

This is addressed by a presheaf model in which the model includes conversion-quotiented type information ("labels") onto the compact elements ("shapes"). So, the model will no longer identify two compact elements Π(A, B,⊥, ∅) and Π(C, D, ⊥, ∅) since the syntactic labels ABCD distinguish them (but in the semantic half, both say something like, "I'm a Π type, but I don't know anything about the domain (⊥), and the table of observations is empty (∅), so I don't know anything about the codomain either"). This redundancy between syntactic and semantic information is sufficient to invert.

Definitional inversion follows from soundness alone: definitional equality in the syntax implies equality in the model (soundness), injectivity in the model implies equality in the model of the components, which includes just enough information to recover defintitional equality in the syntax of the components. To prove soundness, the step functions, which are the compact function elements, (and gain typing information in their tables of observations) are required to be compatible under every future substitution (referred to as "coherent"), requiring some extra bookkeeping.

Definitional inversion includes injectivity of type formers (the diagonal) and no-confusion of type formers (the off-diagonal). Consequences also include uniqueness of typing and uniqueness of sorts.

The Lean code was written with moderate AI assistance. The formalisation details are very much rooted in QIITs, but any mechanisation in, say, agda, would probably be a lot more erratic in AI use.

cc @Mario Carneiro @Meven Lennon-Bertrand

So just to be double clear, you have the same result we have, but for a type theory which adds a proof-irrelevant identity type with Lean's "K-elimination" rule? That's cool! We poked that thing a little bit when working on the paper, but were not quite sure we could model it easily (the model seemed more apt to model a Prop-valued observational equality than what Lean currently does), so in the end we kept that for future work

As for the technique, the way I understand our approach is that the model alone loses a lot of information, and that many things that are not defeq in the syntax become equated in the model. Yet once we build the glued model/logical relation, everything is fine again, because, the first component of the glued model being syntax, equality in the glued model has to be more fine grained than equality in syntax (and in fact because it is a model it has to be coarser, hence they coincide). But what you are saying is that to handle the K reduction rule make the model itself more fine-grained, so that you get better inversion from the domain model alone, rather than from the glued one?
